content: Preterm infants, defined as those born before 37 weeks of post-menstrual age (PMA), often experience delays in achieving the ability to feed orally. The ability to feed orally is considered a critical milestone for determining the timing of hospital discharge and serves as an early indicator of neuromotor integrity and developmental outcomes. Various oral stimulation interventions have been proposed to assist these infants in developing the necessary sucking and oromotor coordination, potentially facilitating earlier oral feeding and reducing the length of hospital stays. This review is an update of a previous analysis conducted in 2016. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of oral stimulation interventions in promoting the attainment of oral feeding in preterm infants born before 37 weeks' PMA. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted in March 2022. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. The search was limited to studies published after 2016, the date of the original review. However, due to delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and staffing shortages, studies identified after September 2020 were not included in the analysis and were instead categorized as Awaiting Classification. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared a defined oral stimulation intervention with no intervention, standard care, sham treatment, or non-oral interventions (e.g., body stroking protocols or gavage adjustment protocols). Eligible studies were required to report at least one of the specified outcomes, which included time to exclusive oral feeding, duration of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) stay, total hospital stay, and duration of parenteral nutrition. Following the updated search, two authors independently screened the titles and abstracts of studies and reviewed full-text articles when necessary to determine eligibility. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by all review authors using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. Studies were grouped into two categories for comparison: oral stimulation versus standard care and oral stimulation versus non-oral or sham interventions. Meta-analyses were performed using a fixed-effect model. The review included 28 RCTs involving a total of 1,831 participants. However, many of the included trials exhibited methodological weaknesses, particularly in allocation concealment and blinding of study personnel. When comparing oral stimulation to standard care, the meta-analysis showed uncertainty regarding whether oral stimulation reduces the time to transition to oral feeding (mean difference [MD] -4.07 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] -4.81 to -3.32 days, 6 studies, 292 infants; I² = 85%, very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency). The duration of NICU stay was not reported in these studies. Similarly, it remains uncertain whether oral stimulation reduces the total duration of hospitalization (MD -4.33 days, 95% CI -5.97 to -2.68 days, 5 studies, 249 infants; I² = 68%, very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency). The duration of parenteral nutrition was also not reported. When comparing oral stimulation to non-oral interventions, the meta-analysis again showed uncertainty regarding whether oral stimulation reduces the time to transition to exclusive oral feeding (MD -7.17 days, 95% CI -8.04 to -6.29 days, 10 studies, 574 infants; I² = 80%, very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision). The duration of NICU stay was not reported in these studies. Oral stimulation may reduce the total duration of hospitalization (MD -6.15 days, 95% CI -8.63 to -3.66 days, 10 studies, 591 infants; I² = 0%, low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias). However, oral stimulation may have little to no effect on the duration of parenteral nutrition exposure (MD -2.85 days, 95% CI -6.13 to 0.42 days, 3 studies, 268 infants; very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision). In conclusion, there remains significant uncertainty regarding the effects of oral stimulation interventions on the time to transition to oral feeding, duration of NICU stay, total hospital stay, and exposure to parenteral nutrition in preterm infants. Although 28 trials were included in this review, only 18 provided data suitable for meta-analysis. The evidence was assessed as being of low or very low certainty due to methodological weaknesses, inconsistency in effect size estimates, and imprecision in pooled estimates. Further well-designed trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy of oral stimulation interventions in preterm infants. Future studies should aim to blind caregivers and outcome assessors to the intervention when possible and should include outcome measures that reflect improvements in oral motor skill development as well as longer-term developmental outcomes beyond six months of age. Currently, 32 ongoing trials are investigating this topic, and their results may provide additional insights into the potential benefits of oral stimulation interventions.
